  • Observed at 19:22:40 Eastern time ET
    United States v. Thomas Clegg (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca8-26-01295 / USCOURTS-ca8-26-01295-0

    FAPD-AI: On November 12, 2026, the Eighth Circuit filed an unpublished per curiam opinion in United States v. Thomas D. Clegg, No. 26-1295, an appeal from the Western District of Missouri. The defendant challenged as substantively unreasonable a within-Guidelines sentence imposed after a jury convicted him of conspiring to commit murder for hire and he pleaded guilty to a firearm offense. The court held that the district court properly considered the 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a) factors, granted counsel leave to withdraw under Anders v. California, and affirmed the sentence. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 19:22:39 Eastern time ET
    Donell Prince v. Priscilla Pajela, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01368 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01368-0

    FAPD-AI: In a consolidated non-precedential per curiam opinion, the Third Circuit affirmed the District of New Jersey's grant of summary judgment to landlord Priscilla Pajela on the claims of pro se appellant Donell Prince. The court upheld the denial of spoliation sanctions, the denial of leave to add Fair Housing Act claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 against three additional individuals, and the summary judgment ruling, which found that the evidence did not establish Pajela's involvement in the alleged exposure. The court also noted that Prince did not adequately develop arguments regarding other claims. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 19:22:39 Eastern time ET
    Santanyo Lewis v. Laurel Harry, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01834 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01834-0

    FAPD-AI: In a non-precedential per curiam opinion, the Third Circuit summarily affirmed the Western District of Pennsylvania's dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) of pro se prisoner Santanyo Lewis's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 complaint alleging deficient medical care at SCI-Greene and SCI-Coal Township. The court held that the complaint did not allege personal involvement by the supervisory defendants and did not plausibly state an Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference claim against nurse Jennifer Beers or Amy Clark. The court also denied Lewis's motion for appointment of counsel. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 19:22:39 Eastern time ET
    Allen Satz v. Ava Satz (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-02106 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-02106-0

    FAPD-AI: In a non-precedential per curiam opinion, the Third Circuit vacated the District of New Jersey's dismissal of pro se appellant Allen Satz's amended complaint against Ava Satz under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine and remanded the case. The court held that the district court did not perform the required claim-by-claim analysis to determine which claims seek review of state-court judgments and which present independent claims, such as certain New Jersey tort claims against Ava Satz. The court left the analysis of other defenses for the district court to perform in the first instance. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 19:22:38 Eastern time ET
    Cheryl Borowski v. Kean University, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02303 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02303-0

    FAPD-AI: On November 12, 2026, the Third Circuit issued a non-precedential opinion in Cheryl Borowski v. Kean University, et al. (No. 25-2303) affirming the District of New Jersey's dismissal of Borowski's claims based on sovereign immunity, qualified immunity, and lack of standing for the declaratory relief sought on her First Amendment claim. The opinion holds that Kean University and its officers in their official capacities are entitled to Eleventh Amendment immunity as an arm of the state. The opinion also addresses claims against New Jersey Civil Service Commission Director Allison Christopher Myers, arising from a letter stating that adjunct professors could not appeal to the Commission. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Donell Prince v. Priscilla Pajela (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02839 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02839-0

    FAPD-AI: On November 12, 2026, the Third Circuit issued a non-precedential per curiam opinion affirming the District of New Jersey's entry of summary judgment against pro se appellant Donell Prince in his action against landlord Priscilla Pajela. The court found no abuse of discretion in the denial of Prince's spoliation sanctions request and no error in denying leave to add Fair Housing Act § 3617 claims against three additional individuals. The court also held that Prince's proffered evidence did not establish Pajela's involvement in the alleged exposure to toxic fumes. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 19:22:38 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Carlos Cegledi (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-03398 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-03398-0

    FAPD-AI: In a non-precedential opinion, the Third Circuit dismissed as moot a pro se appeal by Carlos Cegledi from the Middle District of Pennsylvania's November 17, 2025 denial, without prejudice, of a motion for early termination of supervised release. The court held that the Eastern District of Pennsylvania accepted transfer of jurisdiction under 18 U.S.C. § 3605 on December 15, 2025, so the transferor court could no longer grant the requested relief. The opinion also warned that future filings containing fabricated authorities or quotations may result in sanctions. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01123 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01123-0

    FAPD-AI: In a non-precedential per curiam opinion, the Third Circuit affirmed the District of New Jersey's denial of pro se appellant Ricky Kamdem-Ouaffo's post-judgment motions for leave to seek reconsideration and for recusal of the district judge. The court found no abuse of discretion in the denials, citing a prior filing injunction and the grounds for relief under Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(b). It also held that disagreement with a judge's rulings did not establish a basis for recusal under 28 U.S.C. § 455(a). USCOURTS-SEL-01

      FAPD-AI: On November 12, 2026, the Tenth Circuit issued an order and judgment in Florez v. Blanche, et al. (No. 26-1188) affirming the District of Colorado's dismissal of Joseph M. Florez, a pretrial detainee, sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and Bivens, alleging that 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) violates the Second Amendment and the Bill of Attainder Clauses.   • Observed at 15:47:32 Eastern time ET
    Sabrina Beram v. City of Sedona (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca9-23-15912 / USCOURTS-ca9-23-15912-0

    FAPD-AI: In a published opinion filed November 12, 2026, the Ninth Circuit affirmed in part and reversed in part the District of Arizona's dismissal of Sabrina Beram's action against the City of Sedona, and remanded. The panel held that Beram alleged an Article III injury and had standing to seek injunctive relief based on the city's credible threat of enforcing its ordinance prohibiting sleeping in a vehicle. The panel further held that Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act may cover a failure to provide reasonable accommodation that would allow a person with a disability to comply with a criminal ordinance, and it affirmed dismissal of the Eighth Amendment claim, which Beram abandoned. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:47:32 Eastern time ET
    Philip Hahn v. USA, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-caDC-26-05255 / USCOURTS-caDC-26-05255-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam judgment filed November 12, 2026, the D.C. Circuit affirmed the District of Columbia district court's May 7, 2026 order dismissing Philip Hahn's complaint for lack of jurisdiction. The court held that the United States and Supreme Court staff are immune from damages suits based on official actions of judicial clerks that are an integral part of the judicial process, and that the jurisdictional question is not a factual issue requiring a jury. The Clerk was directed to withhold issuance of the mandate until seven days after resolution of any timely rehearing petition. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:47:32 Eastern time ET
    Darrell Harper v. USA, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-caDC-26-05277 / USCOURTS-caDC-26-05277-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam judgment filed November 12, 2026, the D.C. Circuit affirmed the District of Columbia district court's dismissal of Darrell Harper's complaint against the United States and Donald J. Trump, and denied his motion to appoint counsel. The court held that damages claims against the United States were barred by sovereign immunity, and that the administration was not a proper defendant for claims based entirely on the actions of judicial officers. The court also affirmed on the alternative ground that the complaint sought review of orders of the Southern District of Texas, which the district court lacked jurisdiction to review, and noted that the dismissal was without prejudice to filing a new complaint. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:47:31 Eastern time ET
    Lodestar Energy, Inc., et al v. OWCP, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca6-25-03840 / USCOURTS-ca6-25-03840-0

    FAPD-AI: In an opinion marked not recommended for publication, dated November 12, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit denied the petition for review filed by Lodestar Energy, Inc. and Kentucky Employers' Mutual Insurance of a Benefits Review Board decision affirming an award of survivor benefits under the Black Lung Benefits Act to Bonnie Owens, the widow of miner John Owens. The Administrative Law Judge initially denied benefits in May 2022, the Board vacated and remanded that decision, and on remand the ALJ granted benefits in July 2024 after reweighing the pulmonary function test evidence. The Board affirmed the second decision in September 2025, and the court's standard of review is de novo for legal conclusions and substantial evidence for factual determinations. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:47:30 Eastern time ET
    Weston v. DOJ (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-26-01515 / USCOURTS-ca13-26-01515-0

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Bureau of Justice Assistance's denial of Ashley Weston's claim for death benefits under the Public Safety Officers' Benefits Act of 1976, following her father's July 2015 death from cardiovascular disease after a suspected stroke. The court held that substantial evidence supported the determination that the firefighter did not die in the line of duty, because his track walk and weight lifting did not constitute an official training program under 28 C.F.R. § 32.13 and the fire department had no mandatory fitness policy. The disposition is nonprecedential. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:47:30 Eastern time ET
    US v. Carl Colvin (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca4-25-04155 / USCOURTS-ca4-25-04155-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated November 12, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed the judgment in United States v. Carl Dennis Colvin, a conviction entered on a conditional guilty plea to possession of child sexual abuse material under 18 U.S.C. §§ 2252A(a)(5)(B) and 2252A(b)(2). The appeal challenged the denial of a motion to suppress evidence from a search of a cell phone conducted under a search warrant, along with statements made after that search. The court concluded that officers had probable cause to seize the phone before obtaining the warrant, that probable cause supported the warrant, and that the good-faith exception would apply even if the warrant were deficient. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:47:30 Eastern time ET
    First Service Bank v. Swarek (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-60618 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-60618-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated November 12, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed summary judgment in favor of First Service Bank against pro se defendant Thomas L. Swarek on his guaranty of a $50,000,000 loan, along with the alternative denial of his motion to set aside default. The court held that the participation and servicing agreements established the bank's authority to enforce the full debt, that M S Facilities was not a required party under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 19(a), and that the appellant had forfeited his challenge to the judgment amount by not raising it in the district court. The court also found no abuse of discretion in the district court's reliance on evidence submitted with the summary judgment reply. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-10366 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-10366-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated November 12, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the judgment of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas in an appeal by Jason Stanford, doing business as Motor Carrier No. 1476454 Rollin' Smoke at the Attache, against England Carrier Services, L.L.C.; England Logistics, L.L.C.; CR England, Incorporated; and King of Freight, L.L.C.   • Observed at 15:47:30 Eastern time ET
    Clemons-Ali v. Tulino (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-20195 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-20195-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated November 12, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the dismissal without prejudice of Carey Clemons-Ali's Family and Medical Leave Act suit against Doug Tulino, Acting Postmaster General, for failure to effect service of process by the extended deadline, and affirmed the denial of her Rule 60(b) motion. The court held that the district court did not abuse its discretion, that Clemons-Ali did not seek to show good cause for the service failure until after dismissal, and that her Rule 60(b)(1) and (6) arguments were forfeited or otherwise unsuccessful. The opinion notes that she may refile her claims until the statute of limitations on her FMLA claims has run. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:47:30 Eastern time ET
    Moore v. Dowies (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-26-30256 / USCOURTS-ca5-26-30256-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion dated November 12, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's summary judgment in Cedre Moore v. Sam Dowies et al., which arose from a Fourth Amendment excessive force claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 following Moore's booking into jail. The appeal concerned the summary judgment ruling on the individual capacity claims against the two wardens and the Monell claim against the sheriff, and the court affirmed essentially for the reasons stated in the district court's March 31, 2026 Memorandum Ruling and Order. The district court had dismissed the wardens' official capacity claims under Rule 12(b) and declined supplemental jurisdiction over the state-law claims. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:47:29 Eastern time ET
    Nadine Frakes v. City of Boynton Beach, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-26-10630 / USCOURTS-ca11-26-10630-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the Southern District of Florida's dismissal with prejudice of Nadine Frakes's 42 U.S.C. § 1983 suit against the City of Boynton Beach and four Boynton Beach Police Department members, arising from officers' warrantless entry into her home after her daughter's death in March 2023. The panel held that the individual officers were entitled to qualified immunity on the unreasonable-search claims, that the failure-to-train and supervisory-liability claims were insufficiently pleaded, and that the district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing without leave to amend. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:47:29 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Lavi Rubinstein (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-26-13111 / USCOURTS-ca11-26-13111-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the revocation of Lavi Rubinstein's supervised release and the nine-month term of imprisonment imposed by the Southern District of Florida. The district court found two violations, one for accepting employment with a company that produces visual depictions of sexually explicit conduct and one for failing to notify his probation officer of a change in employment at least ten days in advance. The panel held that Rubinstein's admission to the second violation was sufficient to support revocation, and that he waived any challenge to the sentence's dependence on the first violation. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction Richard L. Drake's appeal from a Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims decision that affirmed a Board of Veterans' Appeals denial of service connection for a bladder disability. The court held that Drake's statutory-interpretation argument under 38 U.S.C. § 5103A(d)(1) was forfeited because it was not fairly raised before the Veterans Court, and that even if considered, the claimed misinterpretation would not alter the outcome because Drake received both an examination and a medical opinion. The disposition is nonprecedential. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: In Zak Shaik v. The opinion addresses whether the complaint's amount-in-controversy and diversity-of-citizenship allegations were sufficient under 28 U.S.C. § 1332 and 28 U.S.C. § 1653, and it reports that the panel found no indication of bad faith in the $75,000 jurisdictional-amount allegation.     USA v. Keenan Johnson (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-13829 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-13829-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment in United States v. Keenan Johnson, in which a former Miami-Dade Police Department detective was convicted of two counts of perjury under 18 U.S.C. § 1623(a) for false testimony about a cell number at a suppression hearing. The panel held that sufficient evidence supported the jury's finding that the false statements were material, because they were capable of influencing the presiding judge's ruling on the motion to suppress. The opinion is designated not for publication. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 15:47:26 Eastern time ET
    Weston Phillips v. Hagerty Insurance Agency, LLC, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-12412 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-12412-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Hagerty Insurance Agency, LLC and Essentia Insurance Company in a suit by Weston Phillips concerning a 1933 Buick insured under a Classic Automobile Policy with a $130,000 guaranteed value. The court found that Hagerty was an insurance agent rather than an insurer, that Essentia's tender of $47,703.13 for repair costs satisfied the policy because the vehicle was not a total or constructive total loss, and that the record did not support a bad faith claim under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6. The court treated the claim for litigation expenses as abandoned. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-13093 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-13093-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Emory Health Inc. on the retaliatory hostile work environment claim that Dr. Melissa Smith brought under the Americans with Disabilities Act.   • Observed at 15:47:25 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Justin Sigmon (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-24-14236 / USCOURTS-ca11-24-14236-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the conviction of Justin Dale Sigmon, entered after a jury trial, for knowingly engaging in sexual contact with his nine-year-old daughter in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 2244(a)(5), an offense arising from an incident on a 2023 cruise to the Bahamas. Sigmon challenged the sufficiency of the evidence on the intent element and the jury's exposure to unredacted forfeiture allegations in the indictment. The court held that the evidence, including video recordings and eyewitness accounts, was sufficient and that the district court did not abuse its discretion in finding the presumption of prejudice rebutted. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Brent Berry, et al v. Native American Services Corporation, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-12009 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-12009-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit granted the Government's unopposed motion for summary reversal and vacated the Middle District of Florida's judgment on the pleadings, which had dismissed False Claims Act qui tam claims brought by Brent Berry and the Gose plaintiffs against Native American Services Corporation and Great American Insurance Group. The district court's sole basis, that the qui tam provisions violate the Appointments Clause, was rejected in United States ex rel. Zafirov v. Florida Medical Associates, LLC.     FAPD-AI: On a 271-135 vote with 26 not voting (Roll No. 322), the House adopted H. Res. 1247, providing for consideration of H.R. 2102, the Major Richard Star Act. As considered, the bill amends sections 1413a and 1414 of title 10, United States Code, to expand combat-related special compensation eligibility to chapter 61 disability retirees with fewer than 20 years of creditable service and to end the concurrent receipt phase-in provisions, effective the first day of the first month after enactment. The bill was made debatable for one hour, divided among the chairs and ranking members of the Committees on Armed Services and Veterans' Affairs or their designees. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Senator Van Hollen submitted amendment SA 6935 to amendment SA 6883 to H.R. 2347, proposing to replace a division of the bill with water quality provisions. Section 1201 would amend section 304(a) of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act to require Federal Register notice, a comment period of at least 60 days, independent external scientific peer review, and state and tribal engagement before a water quality criterion is finalized, and it would amend section 509(b)(1) to reference the definition of 'waters of the United States'. Section 1202 would add subsection (e) to section 401 of the Act, limiting the scope of state certifications to water quality requirements, establishing prefiling meetings, and setting deadlines for acknowledging applications and issuing completeness notices, with certification waived if a certifying authority does not act within the reasonable review period.     FAPD-AI: Senator Bennet submitted amendment SA 6950 to amendment SA 6883 to H.R. 2347, proposing a new Title IV, 'Mining Reform', to be added at the end of division B. The title defines terms including 'casual use,' 'exploration,' 'locatable mineral,' 'mineral activity,' and 'undue degradation,' and it limits the issuance of patents to mining claims for which a patent application was filed by September 30, 1994, with the requirements fully complied with. The title also repeals section 2325 of the Revised Statutes, establishes a $400 annual claim maintenance fee per unpatented claim beginning August 31, 2027, in lieu of assessment work, restricts relocation of relinquished claims for 10 years, and provides for Consumer Price Index adjustments every 5 years. CREC-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: Senators Bennet, Schiff, and Lujan submitted amendment SA 6956 to amendment SA 6883 to H.R. 2347, proposing to replace a section of the bill concerning federal environmental review procedures. The text requires federal agencies to publish draft environmental impact statements and environmental assessments in the Federal Register, with a Tribal consultation period and a public comment period each of not less than 45 days, and it sets deadlines of 1 year for environmental assessments and 2 years for environmental impact statements. The amendment also provides for the adoption of existing documents, a dispute resolution process under the direction of the Chairman whose resolutions are stated to be final and not subject to judicial review, and requirements for key permitting agency personnel to act on delayed determinations.     FAPD-AI: Senator Duckworth, with Senator Grassley, submitted amendment SA 6996, intended to be proposed to amendment SA 6883 to H.R. 2347, and ordered it to lie on the table. The text replaces pages 238 through 269 of the amendment with revisions to section 216 of the Federal Power Act governing Federal Energy Regulatory Commission permits for electric transmission facilities, including state siting authority, consultation requirements, landowner input, rights-of-way procedures under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 71.1, and cost allocation through tariffs.     FAPD-AI: Senator Duckworth submitted amendment SA 6997, intended to be proposed to amendment SA 6883 to H.R. 2347, and ordered it to lie on the table. The text replaces pages 249 through 256 of the amendment with a new subsection (j) of section 216 of the Federal Power Act, directing the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to issue land restoration standards within 180 days of enactment, require on-site inspections by independent professional engineers paid by the permit holder, and set corrective action, civil penalty, and private civil action procedures for violations. The text also adds section 216A to the Federal Power Act, which provides that activities to maintain or increase transmission capacity within covered areas of existing rights-of-way are not treated as major federal actions under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 or as undertakings under section 306108 of title 54, U.S. Code.     Horse Protection (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE · FR-2026-11-13 / 2026-23086

    official summary: On May 8, 2024, the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) of the United States Department of Agriculture published in the Federal Register a final rule that amended the regulations promulgated under the Horse Protection Act (the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule). APHIS is proposing to remove the provisions of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule that have been vacated by court order and proposing to withdraw the remaining non-vacated provisions of the May 2024 Horse Protection final rule to ensure that the regulations afford due process and better align with the Act. APHIS is also proposing to amend the regulations by revising, among other things, the certification requirements for training and licensing of designated qualified persons (DQPs); enhancing DQP inspection procedures and the process for appealing APHIS inspections before any possible disqualification by management; and clarifying that if a horse is determined to be sore, it is disqualified from participating in the class in which the inspection took place and not the entire event. FR-SEL-02

    official summary: This regulation establishes a time-limited tolerance for residues of isocycloseram, including its metabolites and degradates, in or on sunflowers. This action is in response to EPA's authorization of a specific exemption under the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) authorizing use of the pesticide on sunflowers.     official summary: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposes to approve a revision to the Oregon State Implementation Plan (SIP) submitted by the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (ODEQ) on December 17, 2025, for the Portland and Salem/Keizer, Oregon 1979 1-hour ozone maintenance areas. The proposed revision updates ODEQ's requirements in the SIP for Stages I and II vapor recovery systems at gasoline dispensing facilities including: decommissioning existing Stage II systems incompatible with onboard refueling vapor recovery systems; allowing removal from service of Stage II vapor recovery equipment compatible with onboard refueling vapor recovery; and removing the requirement for Stage II vapor recovery at new installations. The proposed revisions also include more widespread adoption of Stage I Enhanced Vapor Recovery, Stage I vapor balance, and enhanced conventional nozzles, among other changes. The EPA is proposing to find that ODEQ's demonstration to remove Stage II requirements is consistent with the Clean Air Act and the EPA's guidance. FR-SEL-02

    Airworthiness Directives; The Boeing Company Airplanes (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION · FR-2026-11-13 / 2026-23198

    official summary: The FAA proposes to adopt a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain The Boeing Company Model 787-8 airplanes. This proposed AD was prompted by a report that certain wing skin outer mold line (OML) penetrating fasteners installed using threaded nuts without cap seals do not provide reliable protection against potential ignition sources when subjected to direct attachment lightning currents. This proposed AD would require inspecting between certain ribs on the left and right wing for wing skin penetrating fasteners with a threaded nut adjacent to the electromagnetic effects (EME) sleeve; inspecting the left and right wing fuel tanks, surge tanks, and dry bays for threaded nuts installed on fasteners that penetrate the upper and lower wing skins; accomplishing the inspection specified in a certain airworthiness limitation (AWL); and applicable on-condition actions. This proposed AD would also require accomplishing concurrent requirements and revising the maintenance program to incorporate the airworthiness limitation task. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. FR-SEL-02

    HR 4930 ENR: To expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights… (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr4930enr

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 4930 (enrolled, 119th Congress, Second Session) amends Section 628A of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1628a) to expand information sharing on suspected intellectual property rights violations in trade. The amendments change the standard from "suspects" to "has a reasonable suspicion," extend covered items to packaging, packing materials, containers, and labels, and authorize U.S. Customs and Border Protection to provide nonpublic information generated by online marketplaces, express consignment operators, freight forwarders, and other entities involved in importation, with notice to the person as prescribed by the Secretary. The Act also adds "any other party with an interest in the merchandise, as determined appropriate by the Commissioner" to the parties eligible under subsection (b). BILLS-SEL-01

    HR 8552 ENR: Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026 (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr8552enr

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 8552 (enrolled, 119th Congress, Second Session), titled "Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026," directs the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to increase, effective December 1, 2026, the dollar amounts for disability compensation and dependency and indemnity compensation under specified provisions of title 38, United States Code, including sections 1114, 1115(1), 1162, 1311(a) through (d), 1313(a), and 1314. Each amount is increased by the same percentage as the Social Security benefit increase effective December 1, 2026, under section 215(i) of the Social Security Act, and the Secretary may administratively adjust certain rates under section 10 of Public Law 85-857. The Secretary must publish the adjusted amounts in the Federal Register by the date required under section 215(i)(2)(D) of the Social Security Act for a determination made during fiscal year 2027. BILLS-SEL-01

    119 HR 3978 PCS: Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119hr3978pcs

    FAPD-AI: H.R. 3978, the Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act, passed the House of Representatives on November 9, 2026, and was received in the Senate and placed on the Senate calendar as Calendar No. 695 on November 10, 2026. The bill amends section 11 v. of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2014(v)) to add reprocessing to the list of activities in the definition of production facility, and to provide that the definition does not include reprocessing spent nuclear fuel in a manner that does not isolate plutonium. The bill's exclusion sits alongside the existing exclusion for uranium enrichment and isotope separation. BILLS-SEL-01

    119 S1759 RS: Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act (opens in a new tab)
    Legislation · govinfo API · BILLS-119s1759rs

    FAPD-AI: S. 1759, the Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act, was introduced by Senator Budd and cosponsors on May 14, 2025, and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. The committee reported the bill with an amendment on November 10, 2026, as Report No. 119-160 and Calendar No. 694. As reported, the bill directs the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration to issue a final rule within 2 years of enactment that creates a noise-based certification standard for civil supersonic aircraft, after consulting with the Administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, with takeoff and landing noise levels not exceeding those required for subsonic aircraft in operation as of enactment, and with a process for periodic review and updating of the standards. BILLS-SEL-01
